title: Respond to and Contain AI Security Incidents
intro: Responding when AI security goes wrong: classifying incidents with an AI-specific taxonomy; escalating to the right mix of security, MLOps, data science, privacy, legal and communications; choosing AI-specific containment such as guardrail changes, throttling, isolation and model rollback; suspending pipelines and terminating agents safely; and preserving model states, weights, configurations and dataset snapshots as evidence.
objectives: Classify, scope and rate AI incidents using a taxonomy that covers injection, jailbreaking, poisoning, model theft, leakage and agent misuse
Run multi-disciplinary escalation by severity, involving legal and privacy early enough to meet notification deadlines
Choose AI-specific containment actions, from guardrail tightening and throttling to isolation, rollback and kill switches
Suspend AI pipelines and terminate agents safely, holding pending actions and cleaning up afterwards
Preserve AI investigative artefacts in order of volatility, with hashes, immutable storage and chain of custody

blocks.title: What kind of AI incident is this?

scenes.title: What kind of AI incident is this?
scenes.say: The first minutes of an incident decide much of what follows. If responders classify an AI incident wrongly, they call the wrong people, run the wrong playbook and may destroy the evidence they need. | This video covers an AI-specific triage taxonomy, and how to use it to scope and prioritise incidents.

scenes.title: Core AI incident categories

items.d: Training, tuning or retrieval data corrupted
Training data, prompts or documents exposed
Tools and permissions used for harm

scenes.say: Six categories cover most AI incidents. | Prompt injection: instructions, often hidden in content the model reads, hijack its task or its tools. | Jailbreaking: someone gets the model to ignore its safety rules and produce content it should refuse. | Data poisoning: training, fine-tuning or retrieval data is corrupted to change the model’s behaviour. | Model theft: weights are stolen, or the model’s behaviour is copied through systematic querying. | Sensitive data leakage: training data, system prompts or retrieved documents are exposed through outputs. | And agent misuse: an agent’s tools and permissions are used to cause harm, whether through manipulation, error or a stolen identity.

scenes.title: Jailbreak or prompt injection?
rows: Hijack the model’s task or tools
scenes.say: Two categories are often confused. A jailbreak is a kind of prompt injection, but responders handle them differently. | In a jailbreak, the attacker is usually the user. In indirect prompt injection, the attacker is often a third party the user never sees. | A jailbreak aims to bypass the model’s safety rules. Injection aims to hijack the model’s task or its tools. | A jailbreak arrives in the prompt itself. Injection often arrives in content the model reads: an email, a web page or a document. | And a jailbreak typically produces harmful content, while injection can send data out or take actions on the victim’s behalf.

scenes.title: Triage in six steps
scenes.say: Triage follows six steps. It starts with an alert or a report: from a detection, a user, a red teamer or the model provider. | Classify the incident using the taxonomy. It may fit more than one category, such as injection that led to data leakage. | Scope it: which systems, models and versions, which data, which users and which agents are involved? | Set severity from impact, how far it has spread, and whether it persists, as poisoning or compromised memory can. | Assign the matching playbook and response team. | And contain the incident, or keep monitoring it, as the playbook directs.

scenes.title: What drives AI incident severity
scenes.say: Six factors drive the severity of an AI incident. | The data involved: personal, regulated or confidential information raises severity quickly. | Actions taken: what agents actually did, such as sending messages, moving money or changing records. | Scale: how many users, customers and systems are affected. | Persistence: poisoned models, corrupted agent memory and tainted indexes keep causing harm until they are cleaned. | Regulatory reach: whether data breach or serious-incident reporting duties apply. | And reversibility: whether the harm can be undone.

items: Classify: injection, jailbreak, poisoning, theft, leakage, agent misuse
Distinguish jailbreaks from indirect injection
Classify, scope, set severity, assign, then contain
Severity: data, actions, scale, persistence, regulation, reversibility
scenes.say: To recap. | Classify AI incidents using a shared taxonomy: prompt injection, jailbreaking, data poisoning, model theft, data leakage and agent misuse. | Distinguish jailbreaks from indirect injection, because the attacker, the route and the harm differ. | Triage by classifying, scoping, setting severity and assigning, before containing. | And set severity from the data involved, actions taken, scale, persistence, regulatory reach and reversibility.

blocks.md:
### An AI incident taxonomy
| Category | Typical indicators | Common first responders | MITRE ATLAS examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prompt injection** (direct or indirect) | Injection detections, unexpected tool calls or destinations, outputs following instructions from documents | SecOps, application team | LLM Prompt Injection |
| **Jailbreaking** | Safety classifier hits, harmful outputs, bursts of rephrased attempts from one account | SecOps, trust and safety, model owner | LLM Jailbreak |
| **Data poisoning** | Behaviour shifts, failing canaries, backdoor-like triggers, suspicious data changes | MLOps, data science, data owner | Poison Training Data |
| **Model theft** | Unusual weight downloads, model storage access, extraction-like query patterns | SecOps, MLOps, legal | Exfiltration via ML inference API; model extraction techniques |
| **Sensitive data leakage** | DLP hits on outputs, canary tokens in responses, system prompt disclosure | SecOps, privacy, data owner, legal | Data and system prompt leakage techniques |
| **Agent misuse** | Out-of-profile tools, bulk actions, unapproved high-impact actions | SecOps, agent owner | AI agent and tool abuse techniques |
| **Supply chain compromise** | Malicious model files or packages, tampered pipelines | SecOps, MLOps, procurement | ML supply chain compromise |
| **Availability and abuse** | Token floods, denial of wallet, capacity exhaustion | SecOps, platform, finance | Cost harvesting, denial of ML service |
| **Harmful output or safety failure** | Dangerous, discriminatory or defamatory outputs without an attacker | Model owner, trust and safety, legal | (Often a limitation, not an attack: Module 6.5) |

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications treats **jailbreaking as a form of prompt injection**. Many organisations still track them separately, because the attacker, delivery route and harm differ, and so do the playbooks. Use ATLAS technique names in incident records so that intelligence, detections and reports line up (Module 5.2). Incidents often span categories: an injection may lead to data leakage through agent misuse, so record a primary category and any secondary ones.

### Scoping questions
- Which applications, model versions, prompts, indexes and agents are involved? (Use the inventory and lineage.)
- Which identities and sessions, and on whose behalf were agents acting?
- What data was accessed, output or sent, and where did it go?
- When did it start? Are poisoned data, compromised memory or a tampered model still in use?
- Did the provider or a supplier report it, and do they hold relevant logs?

### Severity in practice
Combine **impact** (data, actions, people, money, safety), **spread** (users and systems affected) and **persistence** into a severity level that drives escalation (Section 2) and containment (Section 3). Be ready to raise severity as scoping reveals more; AI incidents often look small at first.

pairs: A user coaxes the chatbot into giving instructions it should refuse

Indirect prompt injection

blocks.title: Triage questions
blocks.md: Expect questions that test whether you can **classify** an AI incident correctly (especially **jailbreak versus indirect injection**, and **poisoning versus drift**) and **scope** it using inventory and lineage. Severity depends on **data, actions, scale, persistence, regulation and reversibility**, not on how alarming the output looks.

q.q: A customer support agent starts adding links to an unknown site in its replies. Investigation shows the instructions came from a product review it retrieved. How should the incident be classified?
o: A jailbreak, because the model produced content its safety rules should block
Indirect prompt injection, delivered through retrieved third-party content
Data poisoning, because the model’s training data must have been corrupted
Model theft, because the attacker is copying the model’s behaviour
q.why: Instructions arriving in retrieved third-party content that hijack the model’s task are indirect prompt injection. It isn’t a jailbreak by the user, the training data wasn’t changed, and nothing was stolen.

scenes.title: The right people, fast
scenes.say: No single team can handle a serious AI incident alone. Security knows attacks, MLOps knows the pipelines, data scientists know the model, and lawyers know the clocks that start ticking. | This video covers multi-disciplinary escalation paths for AI incidents.

scenes.title: Who an AI incident needs
scenes.say: A serious AI incident needs six groups. | Security operations leads detection, containment and forensics. | MLOps and platform engineers carry out rollbacks, suspend pipelines and manage serving. | Data scientists analyse what the model did, and how far the impact reaches. | The data owner and privacy team assess which data was affected, and whether it is a personal data breach. | Legal and compliance track notification duties, contracts and legal privilege. | And the business owner and communications team make business decisions and speak to customers and the media.

scenes.title: An escalation path
scenes.say: Here is a typical escalation path. A SOC analyst triages the alert and takes any pre-approved first containment. | An AI incident lead takes charge, coordinating the response and owning the decisions log. | The core team forms: security operations, MLOps and data science, with the model owner. | As severity or data impact grows, the extended team joins: legal, privacy, compliance and communications. | Executives are brought in for major decisions, such as taking a customer-facing service offline. | And external parties are contacted as needed: regulators, the model provider, law enforcement and affected customers.

scenes.title: Escalation by severity
scenes.say: Escalation should scale with severity, and the thresholds should be agreed in advance. | For a low-severity incident, the SOC handles it and informs the model owner by the next working day. | For medium severity, the core AI response team is engaged within about four hours. | For high severity, legal, privacy and communications join within an hour. | And for a critical incident, executives and external parties are engaged immediately. These timings are illustrative; set your own in the incident response plan.

scenes.title: Clocks that may start ticking

events.d: Significant incidents, essential and important entities

scenes.say: Legal and compliance must join early, because notification clocks may start as soon as the organisation becomes aware. | Under NIS2, essential and important entities send an early warning of a significant incident within twenty-four hours. | Under the GDPR, a personal data breach must be notified to the supervisory authority within seventy-two hours, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people. | NIS2 also requires a fuller incident notification within seventy-two hours. | The EU AI Act requires serious incidents involving high-risk AI systems to be reported within fifteen days, or two days for widespread infringements or critical infrastructure, once those obligations apply. | And NIS2 requires a final report within one month.

items: SecOps, MLOps, data science, privacy, legal, business and comms
Named incident lead; core team, then extended team
Escalate by severity, with agreed timings
Bring legal in early: notification clocks may be running
scenes.say: To recap. | AI incidents need security, MLOps, data science, privacy, legal, business and communications working together. | Name an AI incident lead, form a core team, and widen it as the incident grows. | Escalate by severity, with timings agreed in advance. | And bring legal and compliance in early, because notification clocks may already be running.

blocks.md:
### Roles in an AI incident
| Role | Responsibilities in the incident |
|---|---|
| **AI incident lead** | Coordinates the response, sets priorities, owns the timeline and decisions log, and manages escalation |
| **Security operations** | Detection, triage, containment actions, evidence collection, forensics and threat intelligence |
| **MLOps and platform** | Model rollback, pipeline suspension, isolation of serving infrastructure, restoring clean versions |
| **Data science** | Analysing model behaviour, scoping poisoning or leakage, designing safety regression tests (Module 5.6) |
| **Model owner** | Accountable for decisions about the model: restrict, roll back, retire, accept residual risk (Module 5.1) |
| **Data owner and privacy** | Identifying affected data and people, personal data breach assessment, data subject communications |
| **Legal and compliance** | Regulatory notifications, contractual duties (including to and from AI providers), legal privilege, law enforcement liaison |
| **Communications** | Customer, employee and media messages, consistent with legal advice |
| **Providers and suppliers** | Model providers, MCP server and tool vendors, data suppliers: logs, fixes and their own notifications (Module 2.5) |

### Notification duties to know
- **GDPR:** notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach within **72 hours** of becoming aware, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people’s rights and freedoms; notify affected people without undue delay where the risk is high (Articles 33 and 34).
- **NIS2:** for significant incidents, an **early warning within 24 hours**, an **incident notification within 72 hours** and a **final report within one month** (Article 23).
- **EU AI Act (Article 73):** providers of high-risk AI systems report serious incidents within **15 days** of becoming aware, **2 days** for widespread infringements or serious disruption of critical infrastructure, and **10 days** in the event of a death. Following the Digital Omnibus on AI, these duties apply once high-risk obligations take effect (from December 2027 for Annex III systems). Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must already report serious incidents to the AI Office (Article 55).
- **Sector and market rules:** for example, DORA for EU financial entities, and the US SEC rule requiring public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents within four business days of determining materiality.
- **Contracts:** customer contracts and AI provider agreements may set their own notification times (Module 2.5).

### Making escalation work
Pre-agree severity criteria, escalation timings and decision rights; keep **contact lists** with deputies for every role; give the incident lead authority to convene people at any hour; include AI scenarios in exercises (Module 5.1); and use a single, secure channel and **decisions log** for the incident, so everyone sees the same facts.

blocks.title: Escalation questions
blocks.md: The best answers involve **legal and privacy early** when personal data or regulated systems are involved, **escalate by pre-agreed severity criteria**, and keep a **single incident lead** with a **decisions log**. Waiting until the investigation is finished before telling legal is a classic wrong answer, because notification clocks may already be running.

q.q: During an AI incident, the SOC confirms that an assistant exposed customers’ personal data to other users. The team wants to finish its root-cause analysis before involving anyone else. What should happen?
o: Finish the root-cause analysis first, so that the legal team receives complete facts
Escalate to privacy and legal now, because breach notification clocks may be running
Inform the communications team only, so that they can prepare a press statement
Wait to see whether any customers complain before deciding whether to escalate
q.why: A confirmed exposure of personal data may trigger the GDPR’s 72-hour clock from awareness, so privacy and legal must assess it immediately, in parallel with the investigation. Waiting for complete facts or complaints risks missing deadlines.

scenes.title: Stopping the damage
scenes.say: Containment buys time: it stops an incident getting worse while the team works out what happened. AI systems offer containment options that traditional systems don’t, from tightening guardrails to rolling back a model. | This video covers AI-specific containment actions, and how to choose between them.

scenes.title: A ladder of containment options

layers.label: Rate limit or throttle
layers.sub: Per key, account, agent or source

layers.label: Fall back or roll back
layers.sub: Safe fallback, or last known-good model

layers.label: Take it offline
layers.sub: Kill switch, with a manual process

scenes.say: Think of containment as a ladder, from least to most disruptive. | Tighten guardrails: block the attack pattern, the malicious source or the risky topic. | Rate limit or throttle a key, account, agent or source address. | Restrict features: disable risky tools, web browsing, file uploads or long-term memory. | Isolate the endpoint: cut network paths and revoke credentials it uses. | Fall back to a safe alternative, such as a simpler model or a rule-based flow, or roll back to the last known-good model. | And, if necessary, take the system offline with its kill switch, switching to a manual process.

scenes.title: Containment by incident type
rows: Disable risky tools; quarantine the source
Block accounts; tighten filters; rate limit
Rolling back to a poisoned version
Tipping off before evidence is saved
scenes.say: The right containment depends on the incident type. | For prompt injection, disable the risky tools and quarantine the malicious source content. Don’t rely on patching the system prompt alone. | For a jailbreak campaign, block the accounts involved, tighten filters and rate limit. Watch for over-blocking legitimate users. | For data poisoning, roll back the model and freeze data ingestion. Make sure the version you roll back to was trained before the poisoned data arrived. | And for model theft, revoke access and isolate model storage, taking care not to tip off the attacker before evidence is preserved.

scenes.title: Choosing a containment action
scenes.say: Choosing a containment action follows a short sequence. Assess the blast radius: what data, actions and users are at risk, and how fast it is spreading. | Pick the least disruptive option that will actually stop the harm. | Preserve evidence first for anything the action will change, such as snapshotting a model before rolling it back, unless waiting would cause serious harm. | Apply the action with the right authority, and log it in the decisions log. | Verify that the harm is actually stopping, using monitoring. | And communicate with users, owners and partners about what has changed.

scenes.title: Containing an injection, minute by minute

events.d: Agent follows text in a supplier page

scenes.say: Here is containment in practice, for an injection incident. | At two minutes past two, an alert shows a research agent following instructions planted in a supplier’s web page. | Two minutes later, browsing is disabled for that agent only, leaving every other agent working. | The malicious page is blocked at the gateway, so no other agent can read it. | The agent’s traces and memory are captured as evidence. | And forty minutes after the alert, browsing is restored, with content scanning added in front of it.

items: Climb the ladder: guardrails, throttle, restrict, isolate, roll back, offline
Match containment to the incident type
Roll back only to a verified clean version
Preserve evidence, apply with authority, verify, communicate
scenes.say: To recap. | Use a ladder of containment options: tighten guardrails, throttle, restrict features, isolate, fall back or roll back, and take offline. | Match the containment to the incident type. | Roll back only to a version verified as clean. | And preserve evidence first, apply actions with proper authority, verify that they work, and communicate the changes.

blocks.md:
### Containment options in detail
| Action | When it fits | Things to check |
|---|---|---|
| **Guardrail tightening** | Active injection or jailbreak campaigns, leakage of a known pattern | False positives; whether attackers simply rephrase |
| **Rate limiting and throttling** | Extraction, abuse, denial of wallet, automated attacks | Per-identity limits rather than global ones, so legitimate users keep working |
| **Feature restriction** | Agent misuse, injection through browsing or documents | Which business processes depend on the feature |
| **Credential revocation** | Stolen keys or tokens, compromised agents | Every credential type: API keys, OAuth grants, refresh tokens (Module 5.3) |
| **Endpoint isolation** | Compromised serving hosts, model theft in progress | Preserve volatile evidence first where possible |
| **Fallback** | Model unreliable but service needed | Fallbacks must be tested and safe (Module 3.6) |
| **Model rollback** | Poisoning, tampering, unsafe model or prompt update | Roll back to a version **verified** as predating the problem; roll back prompts, guardrails and indexes too if they changed |
| **Kill switch** | Severe, spreading harm with no safer option | Manual process ready; communication plan (Module 5.7) |

### Rollback is more than the model
An AI system’s behaviour depends on its model, system prompt, guardrail configuration, retrieval index and tools. A clean rollback restores **the combination** that was known to be good, which is why configuration as code and versioned indexes matter (Module 5.1). For poisoning, use lineage to find the last model trained before the suspect data arrived, and freeze pipelines so a scheduled retraining doesn’t redeploy the poison (Section 4).

### Containment and evidence
Containment often changes the evidence: rolling back overwrites the running model, cleaning an index deletes poisoned documents, and terminating an agent loses its memory. Where the harm allows, **snapshot first** (Section 5). Where it doesn’t, act, then record exactly what was done and when. For suspected theft or insider activity, consider **quiet containment** first: restrict and monitor while preserving evidence, rather than alerting the attacker.

### Authority and records
Pre-approved containment actions let on-call staff act at once (Module 5.1); more disruptive actions need the incident lead or model owner. Every action goes in the **decisions log**: who decided, what was done, when, and why.

blocks.title: The poisoned support model
blocks.md: A retailer’s support model starts recommending a competitor’s website for certain product questions. Data science finds that 3,000 poisoned examples entered a fine-tuning dataset through a labelling vendor six weeks ago. Since then, the model has been retrained twice, and another retraining is scheduled for tonight.

q.q: What is the BEST containment approach?
o: Roll back to the latest version, then ask the vendor to remove the bad examples
Freeze retraining, snapshot evidence, then roll back to a model trained before the poisoning
Add a guardrail blocking the competitor’s name, and let tonight’s retraining run as planned
Delete the fine-tuning dataset immediately, so the poisoned examples can’t be used again
q.why: Freezing the pipeline stops the poison being redeployed, the snapshot preserves evidence, and lineage identifies a clean model to restore. The latest versions are both poisoned, a name block is a narrow patch, and deleting the dataset destroys evidence.

blocks.title: Containment questions
blocks.md: Choose the **least disruptive action that actually stops the harm**, matched to the incident type. For poisoning, the best answers **freeze pipelines** and **roll back to a verified clean version**. For theft or insiders, think about **preserving evidence** before alerting the attacker. Patching only the system prompt is rarely the best containment.

q.q: An attacker is systematically querying a proprietary model’s API to copy its behaviour. Which containment action is MOST appropriate first?
o: Delete the model and retrain a new one with different data
Throttle and restrict the attacking identities while preserving logs
Make the API free to use, so the attacker loses their advantage
Publish the model weights openly, so that extraction no longer matters
q.why: Targeted throttling and restriction of the identities involved stops further extraction without disrupting legitimate users, and preserved logs support investigation and legal action. The other options are disproportionate or self-defeating.

scenes.title: Pulling the brake
scenes.say: Some AI incidents keep getting worse on their own. A poisoned pipeline retrains and redeploys on schedule, and a hijacked agent keeps acting until someone stops it. | This video covers suspending AI pipelines and terminating agents safely.

scenes.title: Suspend the pipeline or terminate the agent?
scenes.say: Two brakes do different jobs. | Suspend a pipeline when data may be poisoned or a build tampered with. Terminate an agent when it has been hijacked or is acting harmfully. | Suspension stops ingestion, training and deployment jobs. Termination stops sessions, running tasks and scheduled jobs. | When suspending, preserve artefacts, logs and job queues. When terminating, preserve the agent’s memory, its traces and any pending actions. | The main risk of suspension is that stale models stay in service longer. The main risk of termination is leaving transactions half-finished.

scenes.title: Suspending an AI pipeline

items.d: If the pipeline itself is compromised

scenes.say: Suspending a pipeline has six parts. | Freeze ingestion: pause the connectors and data feeds that bring in new data. | Pause scheduled jobs: training, fine-tuning and re-indexing. | Block promotion in the model registry, so no new version can be approved. | Disable deployment triggers, so nothing is released automatically. | Lock artefacts with retention locks, so datasets, models and logs can’t be deleted. | And if the pipeline itself may be compromised, revoke its credentials.

scenes.title: Terminating an agent safely
scenes.say: Terminating an agent safely follows an order. First, stop new work: no new tasks, sessions or scheduled runs. | Revoke its credentials: tokens, keys and delegated grants, so it can’t act even if something is still running. | Hold pending actions, such as queued emails, payments or tickets, for human review. | Snapshot its state: memory, traces and current context, which investigators will need. | End the running tasks, sessions and processes. | And switch to a manual fallback, so people can take over the work the agent was doing.

scenes.title: Cleaning up after a harmful agent

items.d: From traces, in the incident window

scenes.say: After terminating a harmful agent, clean up in six steps. | List every action it took during the incident window, from its traces. | Reverse what you can: issue refunds, recall messages and restore changed records. | Notify the customers, partners and staff who were affected. | Clean the agent’s memory and any data it wrote, removing planted instructions that could re-trigger the incident. | Record actions that can’t be undone, for legal and compliance. | And restart the agent only with approval, after fixes and testing.

items: Suspend pipelines to stop poison or tampering spreading
Freeze ingestion, jobs, promotion and deploys; lock artefacts
Terminate agents: stop work, revoke, hold, snapshot, end, fall back
Reverse actions, clean memory, restart only with approval
scenes.say: To recap. | Suspend pipelines to stop poisoned data or tampered builds spreading into production. | Freeze ingestion, scheduled jobs, promotion and deployments, and lock artefacts against deletion. | Terminate agents in order: stop new work, revoke credentials, hold pending actions, snapshot state, end tasks and fall back to people. | Then reverse what you can, clean memory and data, and restart only with approval.

blocks.md:
### Designing for the brake
Stopping must be **designed in** before an incident:
- **Pipelines** need a documented, tested way to freeze each stage: ingestion connectors, scheduled training and re-indexing, registry promotion and deployment. Retention locks should protect artefacts during investigations.
- **Agents** need an off switch that works regardless of the model’s cooperation: credential revocation at the identity provider or gateway, a central flag the orchestration layer checks before every step, and the ability to end running sessions. Never rely on instructing the agent to stop.
- **Human oversight rules expect this:** the EU AI Act (Article 14) requires high-risk systems to let overseers intervene or interrupt operation through a "stop" button or similar procedure, bringing the system to a halt in a safe state.
- **Pending actions:** queue high-impact actions (payments, external messages, deletions) so they can be held. Make actions **idempotent** and recorded, so reversal is possible.

### Terminating a compromised agent
1. **Stop new work** at the orchestration layer.
2. **Revoke credentials:** API keys, OAuth grants and refresh tokens, delegated tokens and MCP server sessions (Module 4.5).
3. **Hold pending actions** in queues for human review.
4. **Snapshot state:** memory stores, conversation context, plans, traces and tool-call logs (Section 5).
5. **End sessions and processes**, including sub-agents it started.
6. **Fall back** to a manual or simpler automated process.
7. **Reverse and notify:** compensating transactions, message recalls, record restores and notifications to those affected.
8. **Restart only after** root-cause fixes, memory and data cleaning, safety regression tests (Module 5.6) and approval by the agent’s owner.

### Pipeline suspension pitfalls
- **Scheduled jobs** that redeploy a poisoned model overnight because nobody paused them.
- **Partial freezes:** pausing training but not re-indexing, so poisoned documents still reach a RAG system.
- **Lost evidence:** clean-up jobs or retention policies deleting the very data needed for investigation.
- **Long suspensions:** stale models degrade too, so plan how long you can safely run without updates (Module 5.7).

blocks.title: An agent sends payments it shouldn’t
items: Stop and revoke
Block new tasks for the agent, and revoke its payment API credentials at the gateway.
Hold the queue
Hold payments queued by the agent but not yet executed, for review by finance.
Snapshot
Capture its memory, traces and tool-call logs, with hashes, before anything is cleaned.
Reverse and notify
Recall or reverse the payments that can be reversed, and inform affected customers and the bank.
Restart carefully
After the cause is fixed and safety tests pass, the owner approves a restart with tighter limits.

blocks.title: Brake questions
blocks.md: For poisoning or tampered builds, look for **pipeline suspension** that covers **ingestion, scheduled training and re-indexing, promotion and deployment**. For harmful agents, the best answers **revoke credentials** and **stop work at the orchestration layer**, not just ask the agent to stop, then **hold pending actions** and **snapshot state** before cleaning.

q.q: A hijacked procurement agent is sending purchase orders to an unknown supplier. What is the MOST effective FIRST step to stop it?
o: Send the agent a message instructing it to stop all procurement activity
Revoke its credentials and block new tasks at the orchestration layer
Wait for the current batch of orders to finish, then shut the agent down
Ask the supplier to reject further orders from the company
q.why: Revoking credentials and stopping work outside the model halts the agent whatever its state, because a hijacked agent may ignore instructions. Waiting lets harm continue, and relying on the supplier is outside your control.

scenes.title: Keeping the evidence
scenes.sub: Preserving model states, weights, configurations and datasets
scenes.say: AI incidents leave evidence in unusual places: model weights, prompt versions, vector indexes and agent memory. Much of it is overwritten by the very actions that fix the problem. | This video covers preserving investigative artefacts in AI incidents.

scenes.title: AI artefacts to preserve
scenes.say: Six kinds of artefact matter in AI investigations. | Model weights and versions: the exact files that were running, with their hashes and registry records. | Configurations: system prompts, guardrail policies, tool definitions and generation parameters. | Dataset snapshots: training and fine-tuning data, and the contents of retrieval indexes. | Logs and traces: prompts, outputs, tool calls and access records. | Runtime state: agent memory, caches and running containers. | And change records: pipeline runs, approvals and deployments, showing how the system reached its current state.

scenes.title: Preserve in order of volatility
scenes.say: Collect evidence in order of volatility, most fragile first. Runtime state disappears when a session ends or a container restarts, so capture agent memory and session context first. | Then caches and queues, including pending actions that are about to execute. | Then logs and traces, before rotation or retention policies delete them. | Then snapshots of retrieval indexes and datasets, before anyone cleans them. | Then model files and configurations: hash them and lock them in the registry, so a rollback doesn’t destroy the evidence. | And finally the change history from pipelines and approvals, which is usually durable but still worth exporting.

scenes.title: Fixing without destroying
rows: Export before rotation; set a hold
scenes.say: Containment and evidence can coexist. | Snapshot the suspect model before rolling back. Don’t overwrite it. | Copy the index before removing poisoned documents. Don’t delete them in place. | Export logs before they rotate, and apply a legal hold. Don’t rely on default retention. | And hash every item and record its chain of custody. Don’t pass evidence around in chat messages.

blocks.md:
### What to preserve, and why
| Artefact | Why investigators need it |
|---|---|
| **Model weights and registry records** | Prove which model ran, compare with signed versions, analyse backdoors or tampering (Module 5.6) |
| **Configurations** | System prompts, guardrail policies, tool definitions, generation parameters and their versions explain behaviour |
| **Dataset snapshots** | Training and fine-tuning data, labels and manifests show what was poisoned and when |
| **Retrieval index snapshots** | Document versions, embeddings and ingestion records reveal planted content and its source |
| **Logs and traces** | Prompts, outputs, retrieved documents, tool calls and identities reconstruct the attack (Module 5.2) |
| **Runtime state** | Agent memory, conversation context, caches and queues show what the agent "knew" and planned |
| **Infrastructure evidence** | Container images, disk snapshots and cloud audit logs for compromised hosts |
| **Change and access records** | Pipeline runs, approvals, registry changes and access logs show who changed what |
| **Provider-held data** | Hosted model providers may hold usage logs; request preservation early under your contract (Module 2.5) |

### Good practice
- **Order of volatility:** collect the most fragile evidence first (RFC 3227 sets out this principle for digital evidence); for AI that means runtime state, queues and caches before logs, indexes and models.
- **Snapshot before you change:** rollbacks, index cleaning, memory resets and agent termination all destroy evidence. Snapshot first unless waiting would cause serious harm, and record what was done if not.
- **Integrity and custody:** hash every item, store originals in write-once storage, analyse copies, and keep a chain of custody record (Module 5.2; ISO/IEC 27037).
- **Size and practicality:** weights and datasets can be very large. Where a registry already stores an immutable, hashed version, preserving a locked reference plus its hash may be enough, provided retention locks prevent deletion.
- **Non-determinism:** you can’t reproduce a past output by rerunning the model, so preserve recorded outputs and the exact model, configuration and context that produced them.
- **Legal holds:** suspend routine deletion for everything related to the incident, including telemetry, data pipeline staging areas and provider logs.
- **Privacy:** evidence often contains personal data; restrict access to the investigation team and record every access.

blocks.title: Evidence questions
blocks.md: Look for answers that **snapshot before changing** (rollback, cleaning, termination), collect in **order of volatility**, and maintain **hashes, immutable storage and chain of custody**. For AI, remember the less obvious artefacts: **prompts and configurations, index contents and agent memory**. "Fix it first and investigate later" is usually the wrong order unless harm is severe and ongoing.

q.q: The team is about to roll back a model suspected of being tampered with, and to clean poisoned documents from its RAG index. What should happen FIRST?
o: Roll back immediately, then reconstruct the evidence later from monitoring dashboards
Snapshot the suspect model and index, hash them and record custody, then proceed
Delete the poisoned documents first, because they are the main source of harm
Ask the vendor to confirm the tampering before taking any further action
q.why: Rollback and cleaning destroy the evidence needed to prove what happened, so snapshot and hash the model and index first, unless waiting would cause serious harm. Dashboards don’t hold the artefacts, and waiting for the vendor delays containment.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a jailbreak and indirect prompt injection?
o: A jailbreak targets image models; indirect injection targets text models only
A jailbreak is usually by the user; indirect injection often comes via third-party content
Jailbreaks are always harmless experiments; indirect injections are always attacks
There is no difference; the two terms describe exactly the same attack
quiz.why: The attacker and delivery route differ, so do the harms and the playbooks: jailbreaks bypass safety rules, injection hijacks the model’s task or tools.

quiz.q: Why should incidents involving poisoned models be rated higher for persistence?
o: Poisoned models run faster, so they affect more users each minute
The harm continues until the model and its data are cleaned
Poisoned models are always detected by antivirus tools
Persistence ratings decide which vendor must pay for the incident
quiz.why: Poisoning, corrupted memory and tainted indexes keep causing harm on every request until they are removed.

quiz.q: Which question is MOST important when scoping an AI agent incident?
o: Which programming language was used to build the agent framework
What data the agent accessed and what actions it took, on whose behalf
How many other agents the organisation is planning to build next year
Whether the agent’s model was the newest version available at the time
quiz.why: Data accessed and actions taken define the impact, and the delegated identity shows whose authority was used.

quiz.q: Why should legal and privacy join an AI incident early when personal data is exposed?
o: They are the only people allowed to use the incident ticketing system
Notification clocks, such as the GDPR’s 72 hours, may already be running
They must approve every technical containment action before it can be taken
They are responsible for rolling back models in most organisations
quiz.why: Deadlines run from awareness, not from the end of the investigation, so assessment must start in parallel.

quiz.q: Who typically carries out a model rollback during an AI incident?
o: The communications team, after approval from the press office
MLOps or platform engineers, on the decision of the model owner
The legal team, to make sure the rollback meets contractual terms
The model provider’s sales team, under the support contract
quiz.why: MLOps is responsible for executing the rollback, while the model owner is accountable for the decision.

quiz.q: Under NIS2, an entity has sent its early warning of a significant incident. By when must it submit the fuller incident notification?
o: Within one month
Within 72 hours
Within 7 days
Within 24 hours
quiz.why: NIS2 requires an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month.

quiz.q: Why must a rollback after data poisoning target a verified clean version?
o: Older versions are always more accurate than newer ones
Recent versions may also have been trained on the poisoned data
The registry deletes any version that is older than one month
Regulators require organisations to keep only one model version
quiz.why: Lineage shows which versions were trained after the poisoned data arrived; rolling back to one of them restores the poison.

o: Taking a system offline at night, when fewer customers are affected
Restricting and monitoring an attacker without alerting them, to keep evidence
Containing an incident without telling the organisation’s management
Using only automated containment, with no human involvement at all
quiz.why: For theft or insider cases, restricting and watching first preserves evidence and avoids prompting the attacker to destroy traces.

quiz.q: Which containment action is usually the LEAST disruptive?
o: Taking the whole AI service offline with its kill switch
Tightening guardrails to block the specific attack pattern
Rolling back every model in the organisation to last year’s versions
Isolating the entire data centre that hosts the model
quiz.why: Targeted guardrail changes sit at the bottom of the containment ladder; take more disruptive steps only if they don’t stop the harm.

quiz.q: Why should an agent be stopped by revoking credentials rather than by instructing it to stop?
o: Instructions cost far more tokens than credential changes, so they are slower
A hijacked agent may ignore instructions, but can’t act without credentials
Credentials expire automatically after any incident anyway
Revoking credentials also deletes the agent’s memory for investigators
quiz.why: Controls outside the model work whatever the agent’s state; a manipulated model may not follow instructions to stop.

quiz.q: Which step is often missed when suspending an AI pipeline during a poisoning incident?
o: Notifying the vendor that supplied the training hardware
Pausing scheduled retraining and re-indexing jobs as well
Updating the model card to describe the suspected poisoning
Renaming the datasets so that attackers can’t find them
quiz.why: Scheduled jobs can redeploy a poisoned model or re-index poisoned documents overnight if only ingestion is paused.

quiz.q: Why should artefacts be collected in order of volatility?
o: The most valuable evidence is always stored in the very largest files
The most fragile evidence, such as agent memory, disappears first
Volatile evidence is not admissible, so it can be collected last
Collecting large files first makes the investigation cheaper
quiz.why: Runtime state, queues and caches vanish on restart or rotation, so they are captured before durable stores.

quiz.q: Why can’t investigators simply rerun a model to see what it said during an incident?
o: Rerunning models is forbidden under most data protection laws
Outputs are often non-deterministic, and inputs or versions may have changed
Models delete their own outputs automatically after each conversation
Rerunning the model would cost too much in tokens to be worthwhile
quiz.why: Recorded outputs, plus the exact model, configuration and context, are the evidence; reruns can give different answers.

exam.q: An HR assistant begins approving leave requests that managers rejected. Logs show employees added text to their requests telling the assistant that managers had already approved. How should this be classified and handled?
o: As a jailbreak, by blocking the employees from using all AI tools permanently
As prompt injection in request content, restricting tools during investigation
As data poisoning, by retraining the model on a cleaned set of leave requests
As model theft, by revoking the assistant’s access to the HR system entirely
exam.why: Instructions embedded in content the assistant processes, changing its task, are prompt injection. Restricting the approval tool contains it while the investigation and fixes proceed.

exam.q: Model weights for a proprietary fraud model were downloaded at 03:00 by a service account that normally only reads inference logs, and sent to an unknown external IP address. Which category and FIRST concern apply?
o: Data poisoning; retrain the fraud model on fresh data immediately
Model theft; contain the account and preserve evidence of the transfer
Jailbreaking; tighten the guardrails on the fraud model’s outputs
Drift; schedule a performance review of the fraud model for next month
exam.why: Unauthorised copying of weights to an external destination is model theft. Containing the account and preserving evidence come first; the other categories don’t fit.

exam.q: A critical AI incident occurs at 02:00 on a Sunday. The on-call engineer can’t reach anyone with authority to approve taking the customer-facing agent offline. What should have been in place?
o: A rule that critical incidents are only handled during business hours
Pre-agreed escalation paths, deputies and decision rights for each severity
A requirement for the engineer to email the whole company before acting
A policy that customer-facing agents are never taken offline under any circumstances
exam.why: Escalation paths with deputies and pre-agreed decision rights let responders act quickly at any hour. The other options delay or prevent necessary action.

exam.q: A provider of a high-risk AI system learns of a serious incident in which a malfunction contributed to a patient’s death. Once Article 73 applies, what is the maximum time to report it under the EU AI Act?
o: 72 hours
10 days
15 days
30 days
exam.why: Article 73 sets 10 days where a death is involved, 2 days for widespread infringement or critical infrastructure, and 15 days otherwise.

exam.q: A chatbot is being manipulated by a coordinated jailbreak campaign from about 40 accounts. Legitimate customers are unaffected so far. Which containment is MOST appropriate?
o: Take the chatbot offline for all customers until the campaign stops
Block or throttle those accounts and tighten filters, watching for over-blocking
Roll back the chatbot’s model to the version used two years ago
Do nothing, because jailbreaks only ever affect the accounts that carry them out
exam.why: Targeted blocking and filter changes stop the campaign with minimal disruption. A full shutdown is disproportionate, an old model is likely weaker, and jailbreak outputs can still cause harm.

exam.q: After rolling back a support model to fix an incident, the team finds the old model still behaves badly. Investigation shows the system prompt and retrieval index had also changed before the incident. What lesson applies?
o: Model rollbacks never work in practice, so models should always be retrained instead
Roll back the whole known-good set: model, prompt, guardrails and index
System prompts should never be changed once a model is deployed
Retrieval indexes should be deleted during every AI incident
exam.why: Behaviour comes from the combination of model, prompt, guardrails and index, so a clean rollback restores the whole known-good configuration.

exam.q: A poisoning incident is confirmed. The team rolls back the model, but the next morning the poisoned behaviour returns. What MOST likely went wrong?
o: The rollback was performed by the wrong member of the MLOps team
The pipeline wasn’t suspended, so scheduled retraining redeployed the poison
The model provider released an update that reintroduced the poison
Users remembered the poisoned answers, and kept asking the same questions again
exam.why: Without suspending ingestion, scheduled retraining and deployment, the pipeline rebuilds and redeploys a poisoned model.

exam.q: A hijacked agent queued 200 outbound customer emails before it was stopped; 50 had already been sent. What is the BEST next action?
o: Delete the queue and the agent’s logs, so the incident can be closed quickly
Hold the remaining 150 emails, assess the 50 sent, and notify those affected as needed
Release the remaining emails, since the agent has now been stopped and is safe
Restart the agent immediately so that it can send corrected versions of the emails
exam.why: Holding pending actions prevents further harm, and assessing sent messages drives notification and recall. Deleting evidence, releasing the queue or restarting the agent are all unsafe.

exam.q: Investigators need to establish what an AI agent believed its instructions were when it transferred funds. The agent has since been restarted. Which artefact would have been MOST valuable?
o: The agent’s source code repository, showing its latest commits
A snapshot of its memory and context taken before the restart
The model provider’s published model card for the base model
The finance team’s monthly reconciliation report for the account
exam.why: The agent’s memory and context show what instructions it was following, including any planted by an attacker. Restarting without a snapshot destroys this.

exam.q: A team must roll back a tampered model within the hour, but its weights are 400 GB. What is the BEST way to preserve evidence?
o: Skip preservation, because the files are too large to copy in time
Lock the suspect version in the registry with its hash, then roll back
Email the weights to the legal team as an attachment before rolling back
Keep the suspect model running in production until a full copy is made
exam.why: A retention-locked, hashed registry version preserves the evidence without delaying containment. Skipping preservation loses it, email is impractical and insecure, and leaving it running prolongs harm.
